newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn seeks to avoid escalation with Iran.
newsitem.headline: Bonn seeks to avoid escalation with Iran.

text.p: Bonn made clear at the weekend it would seek to avoid stoking a row with Iran over a court ruling that Tehran ordered political killings in Germany, despite a march on its embassy by hundreds of thousands of Iranians.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told Sunday's weekly Welt am Sonntag in his first comment on the crisis that Iran must show respect for international law before Bonn could discuss a fresh start in relations.
But he added: "We do not want an end to relations which have existed for over 100 years and, as upset as we are, we do not want to pour oil on the flames."
Iran on Sunday responded to the withdrawal of all European Union ambassadors except Greece's by announcing it would pull its envoys out of those countries in return.

Hundreds of thousands of Iranians marched on the German embassy in Tehran chanting "Death to Germany, fascist Germany, servant of Zionism". But the demonstration, the second since Friday, remained orderly as police cordoned off the embassy.

Bonn has gone out of its way to say it trusts Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati's assurances that Germans in Iran will come to no harm. The German Foreign Ministry said it still planned to reopen the embassy -- closed since before Thursday's court ruling -- on Monday.

Bonn officials say privately that behind the scenes, Iran has signalled it also does not wish to raise the temperature in the diplomatic stand-off with a country which, until recently, was its biggest trading partner and friend in the West.

They point to the fact that Iran's diplomatic steps, including the ordering out of four German diplomats in return for the expulsion of four Iranians from Germany, have exactly mirrored Bonn's actions, and not gone any further.

Iran's leaders, while attacking Bonn and rejecting the court verdict, have also made clear in their comments that Bonn need not fear a complete freeze in relations. President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani called the row a "passing storm".
Kinkel himself has come under pressure from commentators for doggedly maintaining ties with Iran despite strong suspicions of state terrorism -- until the court forced his hand.
In the interview, he defended the EU policy of "critical dialogue" which he had championed, and which has now been ended.
The policy was supposed to keep communication channels open to encourage more pro-Western elements in the Iranian establishment while not losing sight of human rights.

Kinkel said the contacts had helped to secure Iran's cooperation with international institutions on human rights and on limiting weapons of mass destruction, and its help in freeing German and other Western hostages in Lebanon.

He said Bonn had no option but to act after the ruling by the Berlin court, which on Thursday accused Iran's state president and religious leader of ordering the 1992 killing of four Kurdish Iranian dissidents in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant.
It convicted an Iranian and three Lebanese, sentencing two of them to life for murder.
Germany still has an arrest warrant out for Iran's Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan, accused by the court of organising the assassinations.

German media have speculated that prosecutors might now try to press charges against Velayati, since the court said the foreign minister was one of those who sat on a secret committee which ordered political assassinations.
A spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office would say only that the office would discuss this week whether any further steps were necessary in the light of the court ruling.
